more_info.uses: EU permissions include entire fresh fruit and vegetables, cocoa and chocolate products as covered by directive 2000/36/ec, other confectionery including breath freshening micro-sweets, chewing gum. These permissions depend on the food category and its conditions of use.
more_info.origin: Purified resin secreted by lac insects. Bleaching produces the specified food-grade shellac.
more_info.dietary_restrictions: Derived from an insect secretion; it is unsuitable for vegan diets. Vegetarian acceptance depends on whether insect-derived ingredients are included. Halal and kosher certification was not established by the specification.
more_info.daily_intake: 4 mg/kg body weight/day for physically decoloured wax-free shellac (EFSA, 2024). The same value is temporary for chemically bleached wax-free shellac; it excludes wax-containing shellac.
more_info.side_effects:
Conservative food-use estimates slightly exceeded the limit in some groups, but EFSA did not consider that exceedance a safety concern.
For chemically bleached material, organochlorine impurities remained a data gap in 2024.
more_info.overview: Shellac is classified in food technology as a glazing agent. Its technological role is to provide a surface coating.
